title: First Glow
summary: Wire a red LED straight across the Uno's 5 V and GND rails and watch it let out its magic smoke. This is the mistake every engineer makes exactly once.

briefing.text: Welcome to the bench! Your very first job is to light an LED, and I want you to do it the reckless way.
Run 5 V straight into the LED with nothing in between. Watch what happens — the smoke is the lesson.
Nothing here is really broken, so experiment freely. Reset sim puts every part back together.

learn.title: Why an LED dies on bare 5 V
learn.body:
An LED is not a resistor. Once the voltage across it passes its forward voltage Vf (about 1.8 V for red) it stops resisting and conducts almost everything you give it.

The current is set by whatever resistance is left in the loop:

    I = (Vsrc - Vf) / (R + Rpin + rOn)

With no resistor at all, R = 0 and only the LED's own tiny internal resistance (about 10 Ohm) is left:

    I = (5 V - 1.8 V) / 10 Ohm = 320 mA

A 5 mm LED is rated for 20 mA and dies above about 30 mA. 320 mA is sixteen times its rating — hence the smoke. Next level you will fix it with a single resistor.

objectives.text: Feed the breadboard: 5 V to the red rail, GND to the blue rail

hints.tier1: The breadboard has no power of its own. The two long side strips are rails — run one jumper from the Uno's 5V pin to the red rail and one from GND to the blue rail.

tier2.text: These are the two terminals your jumpers should reach.

objectives.text: Put the LED straight across the rails — anode to 5 V, cathode to GND

hints.tier1: An LED only works one way round. The long leg (anode) faces the positive rail, the short leg (cathode) faces ground.

tier2.text: Drop the LED across two different rows, then jumper each row to a rail.

objectives.text: Run it and release the magic smoke

hints.tier1: Nothing is limiting the current, so the LED will destroy itself the moment power reaches it. Press Run.

tier2.text: The LED must sit directly across 5 V with no resistor anywhere in the loop.

starCriteria.threeText: Blow it up with exactly one part on the board — just the LED

successText: That is what 320 mA through a 20 mA part looks like. You just learned the single most important rule in electronics: something must limit the current.
chipOnSmoke: Ha! Right on schedule. 5 V straight into an LED means about 320 mA through a part rated for 20 mA — sixteen times too much. Next level you get a resistor.
